title: 19. Presidential Election in the United States

segments.text: Americans do not directly elect the president by national popular vote — this is the topic’s single most important, and most commonly misunderstood, fact, and mastering the nomination-to-inauguration flowchart resolves most confusion.

items.text: The constitutionally mandated system of state-based electors, not a direct national popular vote, that formally selects the president.
The House-by-state-delegation procedure used if no candidate achieves an Electoral College majority.
Draw a flowchart from candidate nomination to inauguration; practise explaining precisely how a candidate can win the presidency without the national popular vote.
Do not say Americans directly elect the president by nationwide popular vote.
Do not say each state has electors based only on population; Senate representation adds two electors to every state’s House allocation.
Do not claim the Electoral College can be abolished by an ordinary Act of Congress; a constitutional amendment would be required.
Each state’s electors equal its total senators plus representatives; DC receives electors under the 23rd Amendment.
Most states use winner-take-all allocation; Maine and Nebraska use a district-based variation.
If no candidate has an Electoral College majority, the House chooses the president by state delegations under the 12th Amendment.
Master the process as a flowchart, and be able to explain precisely how the Electoral College can diverge from the national popular vote.
Abolishing the Electoral College would require a constitutional amendment, not ordinary legislation — a frequently tested precision point.
